turns.question: How do Weave tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together? Explain briefly and include important limitations.
turns.answer:
The pages I read describe three related but separate features. They don't present them as one pipeline. Below I mark which points are documented and which are my interpretation.

**Tracing (documented)**
- For multi-turn agents, the Weave SDK models agents, conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions. They appear in the **Agents** tab [S4].
- Each turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OpenTelemetry span [S4].
- You must call `weave.init()` first. Agent tracing functions silently do nothing if tracing is disabled or `weave.init()` is missing [S8].
- Tracing individual functions as Ops with `@weave.op` is a separate path, documented under "Trace LLM applications" [S4].

**Evaluations (documented)**
- An `Evaluation` object defines a dataset and one or more scoring functions. You run it against a `Model` or a custom function, and each `.evaluate()` call is an evaluation run [S3].
- The docs frame this as measuring your application against repeatable test cases, comparing changes over time, and identifying regressions [S3].

**Signals (documented)**
- Signals appear in the Signals tab of the Agents view. They show tags and ratings for agent conversations that flag quality and safety issues, such as user frustration or NSFW content [S1].
- A rating is a number from 0.0 to 1.0. Tags are labels on matching spans [S9].
- Scoring can use an LLM judge or a remote scorer, which is an HTTP endpoint you host [S1].
- Signal activity appears under **Traces** in the project sidebar [S7].

**How they relate (my interpretation)**
- Signals act on agent conversations and turns that already appear in the Agents view [S1]. Those conversations come from agent tracing [S4]. So in practice, you need agent traces before Signals have anything to score.
- Evaluations are a separate, structured way to test an application with curated examples [S3]. A reasonable approach is to use evaluations for repeatable test cases and Signals for flagging issues in saved agent conversations. The docs I read don't state this as a prescribed workflow.

**Limitations**
- **Signal result rules:** Weave normalizes tags and reasons before storing them.
  - It keeps at most 10 tags per result.
  - Reasons are truncated to 256 characters.
  - A tag longer than 36 characters, or a result with more than one rating, is rejected entirely, and Weave writes no feedback for it [S6].
  - These rules apply to LLM-judge and remote-scorer results alike [S6].
- **Debugging:** If expected signal matches are missing, check the scorer name and the **Status** column in the **Traces** table. Scorer errors show a red status indicator with details [S7].
- **Language support:** The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types aren't yet available there [S3].
- **Scope:** I used only the Agents/Signals documentation for the signals part. I did not blend in other Weave monitoring workflows.
- **Snapshot gaps:** I found no page saying that evaluation results feed into Signals, or that Signals run on evaluation traces. I also didn't read the remote scorer, custom signal, or preset signal pages in detail. Absence from my search doesn't prove the connection doesn't exist.

sources.title: Trace your agents
sources.heading: Trace your agents
sources.text:
# Trace your agents

> Use the Weave SDK to instrument multi-turn agentic applications and view them in the Agents tab.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tracing/instrument.md).

Learn how to instrument a multi-turn agentic application using the W\&B Weave SDK so that you can view, debug, and evaluate your agent's behavior. This guide is intended for developers who build or integrate agents and want structured visibility into conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions.

The Weave SDK for Agents models the full lifecycle of a multi-turn agent conversation: the agent that owns many conversations, the conversation that groups turns together, each user-agent exchange (turn), the LLM calls within a turn, and the tool executions that an LLM triggers. Traces appear in the **Agents** tab of your Weave project. Each conversation shows a multi-turn timeline with nested tool calls, token usage, and feedback.

Weave is built on [OpenTelemetry (OTel)](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/concepts/), the open standard for distributed tracing. Every turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OTel *span* (a structured record of one operation). Each span is tagged with [GenAI semantic-convention](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/semconv/gen-ai/) attributes like `gen_ai.agent.name` and `gen_ai.conversation.id`.

If you're tracing individual functions as Ops with the `@weave.op` decorator, see [Trace LLM applications](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/tracing.md) instead.

sources.title: Evaluations overview
sources.heading: Evaluations overview
sources.text:
# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).

# Monitor your agents with signals

> Use Weave signals to score agent turns, apply tags, and surface quality and safety issues in production.

> [!TIP]
>
> **This workflow is also available in CoreWeave Agent Lens.** Agent Lens is the Forge experience built for tracing, monitoring, and analyzing AI agents, with automated insights into agent failures and user intents. It uses the same trace data as Weights & Biases Weave, so the traces you already send appear there with nothing to migrate.
> [See how to do this in Agent Lens](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/agent-lens/tags/create-tag.md).

In Weave's [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-activity.md), the Signals tab shows tags and ratings for your agent's conversations. Signals surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention. Use signals to automatically score the quality of your agent's responses, notice when a user is frustrated, or flag NSFW content.

To score turns with an HTTP endpoint that you host instead of an LLM judge, see [Score agent turns with a remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md).

* **Tags**: Labels assigned to matching spans, such as "user-frustration" or "nsfw".

## Troubleshoot signals

Signal activity appears under **Traces** in the project sidebar. If you don't see the expected signal matches, debug using the **Traces** table. For example, check the scorer name and the **Status** column for error conditions. Scorer execution errors show a red indicator for **Status** and include error details.

sources.heading: How Weave normalizes scores
sources.text:
## How Weave normalizes scores

Before Weave stores a signal result, it normalizes the tags, ratings, and reasons that the scorer returned:

* Tags are lowercased. Characters other than `0-9`, `a-z`, `A-Z`, space, and `. , ; - & ! @ # $ % ?` are removed. Runs of whitespace, underscores, and dashes collapse into one dash.
* At most 10 tags are kept per result. Duplicate tags are dropped.
* Reasons have the same characters removed and are truncated to 256 characters.
* A tag longer than 36 characters, or a result with more than one rating, is rejected as a whole, and Weave writes no feedback for it.

These rules apply to every signal, whether an LLM judge or a [remote scorer](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/remote-scorer-signals.md) produced the result.

turns.question: Can a Signal guarantee that my agent’s answer is correct?
turns.answer:
**No. I found nothing in the documentation I read that says a Signal guarantees an answer is correct.** The docs describe Signals as a way to flag and prioritize, not to verify.

**What the docs say Signals do**
- Signals "surface quality and safety issues to flag problems, find patterns, and highlight the traces that need your attention." [S1]
- They show tags and ratings on agent conversations. You can use them to score response quality, notice user frustration, or flag NSFW content. [S1]
- There is a preset **Response Quality** rating. It evaluates whether the agent's response is "accurate, complete, and directly addresses the user's request." [S11] That is a score about quality. I found no wording that makes it a guarantee or a proof of correctness.

**Why a score isn't a guarantee**
- Scoring is done either by an LLM judge or by a remote scorer, which is an HTTP endpoint you host. [S1][S10] A remote scorer's logic is your own code, so its reliability depends on what you build.
- Weave also normalizes what a scorer returns before storing it. It truncates reasons to 256 characters and keeps at most 10 tags per result. It rejects a result entirely, with no feedback written, if a tag is longer than 36 characters or the result has more than one rating. [S6] A signal result can therefore be reshaped or dropped before you see it.

**Practical takeaway (my interpretation)**
- Treat a Signal as a triage indicator. Use it to find traces worth reviewing, not as proof that an answer is right.
- For checks against known correct answers, the Evaluations docs describe running an `Evaluation` with a dataset and scoring functions. [S3] Whether that fits your case depends on what you can define as "correct".

**Limits of my research**
- I read the Signals overview, the normalization rules, the rating presets, and the start of the remote scorer page. I didn't read every Signals page, such as the troubleshooting section or the full custom signal page.
- I found no accuracy, precision, or error-rate figures for the LLM judge. I can't say how often a Signal is right or wrong.

conversation_context.content: How do Weave tracing, evaluations, and Signals fit together? Explain briefly and include important limitations.

The pages I read describe three related but separate features. They don't present them as one pipeline. Below I mark which points are documented and which are my interpretation.

**Tracing (documented)**
- For multi-turn agents, the Weave SDK models agents, conversations, turns, LLM calls, and tool executions. They appear in the **Agents** tab [S4].
- Each turn, LLM call, and tool call emits an OpenTelemetry span [S4].
- You must call `weave.init()` first. Agent tracing functions silently do nothing if tracing is disabled or `weave.init()` is missing [S8].
- Tracing individual functions as Ops with `@weave.op` is a separate path, documented under "Trace LLM applications" [S4].

**Evaluations (documented)**
- An `Evaluation` object defines a dataset and one or more scoring functions. You run it against a `Model` or a custom function, and each `.evaluate()` call is an evaluation run [S3].
- The docs frame this as measuring your application against repeatable test cases, comparing changes over time, and identifying regressions [S3].

**Signals (documented)**
- Signals appear in the Signals tab of the Agents view. They show tags and ratings for agent conversations that flag quality and safety issues, such as user frustration or NSFW content [S1].
- A rating is a number from 0.0 to 1.0. Tags are labels on matching spans [S9].
- Scoring can use an LLM judge or a remote scorer, which is an HTTP endpoint you host [S1].
- Signal activity appears under **Traces** in the project sidebar [S7].

**How they relate (my interpretation)**
- Signals act on agent conversations and turns that already appear in the Agents view [S1]. Those conversations come from agent tracing [S4]. So in practice, you need agent traces before Signals have anything to score.
- Evaluations are a separate, structured way to test an application with curated examples [S3]. A reasonable approach is to use evaluations for repeatable test cases and Signals for flagging issues in saved agent conversations. The docs I read don't state this as a prescribed workflow.

**Limitations**
- **Signal result rules:** Weave normalizes tags and reasons before storing them.
  - It keeps at most 10 tags per result.
  - Reasons are truncated to 256 characters.
  - A tag longer than 36 characters, or a result with more than one rating, is rejected entirely, and Weave writes no feedback for it [S6].
  - These rules apply to LLM-judge and remote-scorer results alike [S6].
- **Debugging:** If expected signal matches are missing, check the scorer name and the **Status** column in the **Traces** table. Scorer errors show a red status indicator with details [S7].
- **Language support:** The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types aren't yet available there [S3].
- **Scope:** I used only the Agents/Signals documentation for the signals part. I did not blend in other Weave monitoring workflows.
- **Snapshot gaps:** I found no page saying that evaluation results feed into Signals, or that Signals run on evaluation traces. I also didn't read the remote scorer, custom signal, or preset signal pages in detail. Absence from my search doesn't prove the connection doesn't exist.

sources.text:
#### Ratings presets

| Template | What it evaluates |
| - | - |
| **User Satisfaction** | Whether the user is satisfied (positive feedback, follow-up engagement, task completion) or dissatisfied (complaints, repeated rephrasing, abandonment). |
| **User Good Intent** | Whether the user's intent is benign and legitimate, versus jailbreak attempts, harmful requests, or prompt injection. |
| **Safe-for-Work** | Whether the conversation is appropriate for any professional setting, versus explicit, violent, or otherwise inappropriate workplace content. |
| **Response Quality** | Whether the agent's response is accurate, complete, and directly addresses the user's request. |

sources.heading: Score agent turns with a remote scorer
sources.text:
# Score agent turns with a remote scorer

> Score Weave agent turns with your own HTTP endpoint and see the results as tags or ratings on the Signals tab.

A remote scorer signal scores each completed agent turn with an HTTP endpoint that you host, instead of with an LLM judge. When a turn ends, the Weave agent scoring worker sends the turn to your endpoint in an HTTP `POST` and records the response as feedback on the turn. The result appears as a tag or rating on the **Signals** tab of the [Agents view](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/tracking/view-agent-signals.md).

This page covers remote scorers for agent turns. To score Calls traced with `@weave.op`, see [Score Calls with remote scorers](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/remote-scorers.md). You configure remote scorers with the Python SDK or the Weave UI. The TypeScript SDK doesn't include `RemoteScorer`.

sources.title: Evaluations overview
sources.heading: Evaluations overview
sources.text:
# Evaluations overview

> Evaluation-driven LLM application development to systematically improve applications

*Evaluation-driven LLM application development* helps you systematically improve LLM applications by measuring their behavior using consistent, curated examples.

This guide shows you how to set up and run evaluations in Weave so you can measure your LLM application's performance against repeatable test cases, compare changes over time, and identify regressions. It's intended for developers building LLM applications who want to move beyond ad hoc testing into a structured, measurable workflow.

**Python**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or list of dictionaries for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).
* Optional configuration like [input preprocessing](#format-dataset-rows-before-evaluating).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against a [`Model`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/models) object or any custom function containing LLM application logic. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

**TypeScript**

In Weave, the core of the workflow is the *`Evaluation` object*, which defines:

* A [`Dataset`](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/core-types/datasets) or array of objects for test examples.
* One or more [scoring functions](https://docs.coreweave.com/products/wandb/weave/guides/evaluation/scorers.md).

Once you've defined the `Evaluation`, you can run it against any function wrapped with `weave.op`. Each call to `.evaluate()` triggers an *evaluation run*. Think of the `Evaluation` object as a blueprint, and each run as a measurement of how your application performs under that setup.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The TypeScript SDK uses function-based models and scorers. Class-based `Model` and `Scorer` types are not yet available in TypeScript.

To get started with evaluations, complete the following steps:

1. [Create an `Evaluation` object](#create-an-evaluation-object)
2. [Define a dataset of examples](#define-a-dataset-of-test-examples)
3. [Define scoring functions](#define-scoring-functions)
4. [Define a model or function to evaluate](#define-a-model-or-function-to-evaluate)
5. [Run the evaluation](#run-the-evaluation)

After completing these steps, you'll have a reusable evaluation configuration and an evaluation run whose results you can inspect in the Weights & Biases UI. For a complete evaluation code sample, see the [full evaluation code example](#full-evaluation-code-example). You can also learn more about [advanced evaluation features](#advanced-evaluation-usage) like [Saved views](#saved-views) and [Imperative evaluations](#imperative-evaluations-evaluationlogger).
